case_info.scenario: A 3-year-old previously healthy boy presented to the dental office for gum bleeding that developed 2 weeks prior to presentation. His parents reported dark spots on his gums that appeared spontaneously over several days and bleeding during teeth brushing. He had no preceding oral trauma and no recent infections. One week after onset of these oral symptoms, he developed a limp in the right leg. His parents also noticed he had difficulty standing up after sitting down to play. He was evaluated by a pediatrician, who diagnosed transient synovitis of the hip due to a viral infection. Findings on a radiograph of the right hip were normal. During the week prior to presentation, the patient developed spontaneous gingival bleeding and increased bilateral limb weakness with inability to bear weight. On presentation to the dental office, he appeared irritable. Physical examination revealed generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous gingival bleeding. He had no lesions on his lips and no edema or exudate in the oropharynx (Figure). The patient’s parents reported that he took no regular medications, had no recent use of aspirin or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and that his diet was limited to primarily chicken nuggets and milk.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.
